title: Inverted Left Half Pyramid
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell space-or-star checks versus building the gap and star regions directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, print a right aligned triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains i minus 1 leading spaces followed by n minus i plus 1 stars, so the widest row comes first, flush against the right edge, and every row after it shrinks by one star while its leading gap grows by one space.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a right aligned triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains i minus 1 leading spaces followed by n minus i plus 1 stars, so the widest row comes first and every row after it shrinks by one star while staying flush against the right edge.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Right Aligned Triangle, Flipped
blocks.text: This is the same shrinking triangle seen with the plain left aligned version, except every row is pushed against a wall on the right instead of the left. The first row needs no padding at all, and every row after it needs one more space than the row before, exactly enough to keep the shrinking star region flush against that same right wall.

blocks.caption: Row i is i minus 1 spaces followed by n minus i plus 1 stars

Before writing any code, it helps to notice exactly which formulas from earlier, related patterns are being reused here, and which ones have reversed.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This shape looks new, but it is really the left half pyramid flipped both top to bottom and formula by formula, not just one property changing but two at once.

Observation 2: In the left half pyramid, the gap shrank as i grew, n minus i, while the stars grew as i grew, i itself. Here, both directions reverse: the gap grows as i grows, i minus 1, while the stars shrink as i grows, n minus i plus 1.

Observation 3: Even though two formulas changed instead of one, each row's exact gap length and exact star length are both still fully known before that row is built, so nothing about the underlying technique needs to change.

Observation 4: The same direct-construction idea, build each region in one operation using its known length, still applies to both the gap and the star region, and every row can still be joined and printed with a single call at the end.
That reasoning already tells us this is not a harder problem, just two already-known formulas, both reversed, combined the same way as before.

Use an outer loop for each row i, and an inner loop that checks every one of the n column positions, deciding for each one individually whether it still falls inside the leading gap or has reached the star region.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Inside that, check every one of the n column positions.
If the position is still within the first i minus 1 columns, print a space.
Otherwise, print a star.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every column position and decide space or star

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every one of the n column positions is checked individually against the boundary i minus 1, so the decision between space and star is made fresh on every single cell, even though that boundary never changes within a row.

The comparison j less than i minus 1 encodes the entire gap-versus-star boundary as a single condition, making it easy to see exactly where the split happens, at the cost of repeating that same check n times per row.
The line break happens once per outer iteration, exactly mirroring every other pattern in this division, only the per cell decision inside the row is new here.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column position in every row is individually checked and assigned the right character.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since all n columns are checked in every one of the n rows.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking every column position one at a time wastes a per cell decision that never changes within a row, since the exact split point between spaces and stars for row i is already known before the row even starts. Both regions can instead be built directly in one operation each, with no per cell checking at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the same boundary decision, is this column still in the gap, gets re-evaluated n times per row even though it only actually changes value once, at column i minus 1.

What stays the same as the left half pyramid: the underlying insight, both the gap length and the star length are known before the row starts, so both regions can be built directly.

What actually changes here: only the two formulas themselves, the gap grows as i minus 1 instead of shrinking as n minus i, and the stars shrink as n minus i plus 1 instead of growing as i.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a repeat operation still builds each region in one step regardless of which formula computed its length, and concatenating the two regions still produces the full row.

The core idea: build the growing gap directly at length i minus 1, build the shrinking star region directly at length n minus i plus 1, concatenate them, then print the row once.

For each row i, build the leading gap and the star region directly, using one operation for the i minus 1 spaces and another for the n minus i plus 1 stars, then concatenate them into a single row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row i, build the leading gap and the star region directly, one operation each, then concatenate them into a single row string and print it once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the spaces and stars directly, one print call per row

blocks.text: This works because both of row i's region lengths, i minus 1 for the gap and n minus i plus 1 for the stars, are fully known ahead of time, only their formulas have reversed compared to the left half pyramid; a direct repeat operation still constructs each region in one step, with no dependence on any other row. As i increases from 1 to n, the gap length i minus 1 grows from 0 up to n minus 1, while the star length n minus i plus 1 shrinks from n down to 1, and concatenating the two produces exactly the right row every time.

items: The gap length is computed as i minus 1 and the star length as n minus i plus 1, directly inside the outer loop, reversing both formulas from the left half pyramid at once.

Two direct repeat operations construct the gap and the star region separately, exactly the same construction technique used everywhere else in this division, then concatenation joins them into the finished row.

Each row is printed immediately after being built, one output call per row, with both the growing gap and the shrinking stars handled entirely by their formulas, not by any special casing in the loop itself.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own growing gap length, i minus 1, and shrinking star length, n minus i plus 1, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is deferring output until every row exists.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete right aligned pattern as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole triangle, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: This pattern combines two ideas already seen separately: a shrinking row length, and a right aligned layout that needs a growing leading gap. Once both formulas are known for a given row, checking every column position individually adds nothing, building each region directly is both clearer and cheaper.

items: Mixing up which formula shrinks and which one grows, the gap grows with i while the star region shrinks with i.
Off by one errors, since row i needs exactly i minus 1 spaces, not i or i minus 2.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: Noticing that a new pattern is really just a known one with one formula flipped, here the row length formula from the shrinking pyramid combined with the gap formula from the right aligned pyramid, is a fast way to derive the right per row formula without working it out from scratch.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this different from the left half pyramid", think: both formulas reverse direction at once, the gap grows instead of shrinking and the stars shrink instead of growing.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every column", think: build the gap and the star region directly, using their known lengths.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing that combines two formulas at once, a growing leading gap and a shrinking star region, the mirror image of the left half pyramid, built directly instead of checked cell by cell.

Core Idea: row i always needs exactly i minus 1 spaces and n minus i plus 1 stars, both lengths known before that row is built, so two direct repeat operations construct each region in one step, and joining every row allows a single output call.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: when two related formulas both reverse at once, the underlying technique still does not need to change, only the two numbers being computed.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape; recognizing which formulas transfer unchanged and which ones flip is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: same direct gap-plus-stars construction as the left half pyramid, just with i minus 1 and n minus i plus 1 instead of n minus i and i.
